name: Zime-Mesme
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Wolff, Ekkehard. 1983. Tonogenese in tschadischen Sprachen. Afrika und Übersee 66:203-220 (Google/UC Library scan of A&Ü Bd. 66-67, archive.org id afrikaundbersee00hambgoog, full view; scanned). Supporting: Shryock, Aaron. 1997. The classification of the Masa group of languages. Studies in African Linguistics 26(1):29-62 (open PDF).
catalog_locator: Wolff 1983 p.209 (scan), p.213, p.217 fn.3 and fn.6; accent passages checked at p.215 (Lamang only) and p.216 (Chadic prehistory). Shryock 1997 p.47, Appendix B.
catalog_quote: [Wolff 1983:209] Da alle der im folgenden imtersuchten [scan: untersuchten] Sprachen in der Literatur als „Tonsprachen'' bezeichnet werden, mag es hier genügen, das jeweilige nicht*distinktive [nicht-distinktive] tonale Subsystem herauszuarbeiten. Aus Gründen des zur Verfügung stehenden Raumes muß hier auf eine Beweisföhrung [Beweisführung] bei drei Sprachen (Zime-Mesme, Mulwi, Lamang) verzichtet werden; diese wird an anderer Stelle (Wolff 1983 b, 1983 c, im Druck) en detaU [detail] nachgeliefert. [p.213] Ohne an dieser Stelle im einzelnen auf die Situation im Zime eingehen zu können (vgl. dazu WoUT [Wolff] 1983 c), läßt sich doch so viel sagen, daß dort die tonalen Verhältnisse im sog. Imperfektivstamm [fn. 6] des Verbums die Klasse des anlautenden Konsonanten reflektieren, und zwar in viel weitergehendem Maße, als dies aus Jungraithmayrs Beschreibung (1978) hervorgeht. [p.217 fn. 6] Es handelt sich bei den „Imperfektivstämmen'' im Zime-Mesme nicht um mittels tonaler Veränderungen abgeleiteten „Aspektstamm II" (Jungraithmayr), sondern um das Verbum in seiner lexikalischen Grundform. [Shryock 1997:47] Tone has not been reconstructed. The tone patterns of verbs are not indicated because tone has a grammatical function in these languages, indicating the aspect of the verb (cf. [Jungraithmayr 1978a, Caïtucoli 1983]). For the nouns, however, tone is lexical

new_statements.translation: Since all of the languages examined below [including Zime-Mesme] are described in the literature as 'tone languages', it may suffice here to work out the respective non-distinctive tonal subsystem. [...] Without being able to go into the situation in Zime in detail here (cf. Wolff 1983c), this much can be said: there the tonal relations in the so-called imperfective stem of the verb reflect the class of the initial consonant, and to a much greater extent than emerges from Jungraithmayr's description (1978).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Zime-Mesme is treated as a tone language (lexical tone on nouns, grammatical/aspectual tone on verbs per Shryock 1997 p.47; verb-stem tone largely predictable from initial-consonant class per Wolff 1983). No accessible source says anything about word stress or accent placement in Mesme.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; Wolff notes tonal 'dualism' (grammatical morphemes carry distinctive tone while lexical root tone is consonant-conditioned).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern tone in verb stems and nouns, not stress; comparative article drawing on Wolff's own then-unpublished analysis of Zime-Mesme (published 1985) and Jungraithmayr 1978. The dedicated phonology (Kieschke 1990) was not accessible, so whether Mesme has a (demarcative) stress remains undetermined.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources use 'Zime-Mesme' / 'Zime (Mesme)' for the Kélo-area Chadian variety = Glottolog mesm1239 [zim]; 'Zime' alone is ambiguous and in Sachnine 1982, Roberts 2025 and Shay 2019 refers to the sister South-Masa languages Heɗe/Lamé [hed] and Pévé [lme], which were not used for the statement.

sources.note: No stress statement for Zime-Mesme. Treats Zime-Mesme as one of the Chadic 'Tonsprachen' (p.209), with tone in the imperfective verb stem largely predictable from the class of the initial consonant (p.213, fn.3 and fn.6 p.217, citing Jungraithmayr 1978 and Wolff 1983c = the later A&Ü 68 paper). 'Akzent' is discussed only for Lamang.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. p.33 places Zime (Mesme) in the southern Masa subgroup; p.47 (Appendix B): 'Tone has not been reconstructed. The tone patterns of verbs are not indicated because tone has a grammatical function in these languages, indicating the aspect of the verb.. For the nouns, however, tone is lexical'. Lists the Mesme primary sources (Kieschke 1990, Hufnagel 1986, Jungraithmayr 1978a).

tone.says: Record only (IRD MODS record, subject descriptor TON): likely restates, in English, the argument of 'Tonogenese in tschadischen Sprachen' - consonant classes (depressor vs non-depressor) condition tone in Chadic verb stems, with Zime-Mesme imperfective-stem tone predictable from the stem-initial consonant - and draws the implications for Afroasiatic tonogenesis; whether it tabulates the Mesme tone inventory could not be seen.
